claims.text: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW has a single-phase BCC structure.
Equal-atomic NbMoTaW has excellent high-temperature mechanical properties.
Equal-atomic NbMoTaW has very poor room-temperature ductility.
The irradiation resistance of NbMoTaW has been predicted by first-principles calculations.
Approximately 0.5 at% Hf should be added to NbMoTaW.
Keeping Hf below 1 at% will avoid additional phase formation in NbMoTaW.
Trace Hf will subtly modify the local atomic environment of NbMoTaW.
Trace Hf will reduce the Peierls barrier for dislocation glide in NbMoTaW.
Approximately 0.5 at% Hf will not cause significant lattice distortion or secondary-phase precipitation in NbMoTaW.
A reduced Peierls barrier lowers the activation energy for dislocation motion and increases dislocation mobility.
Increased dislocation mobility will enhance the room-temperature plasticity of NbMoTaW.
The low Hf concentration will leave the bulk BCC structure essentially unchanged.
The low Hf concentration will leave irradiation-relevant defect-recombination dynamics essentially unchanged.
Hf-modified NbMoTaW will show significantly increased room-temperature plastic strain and fracture toughness relative to untreated NbMoTaW.
Hf-modified NbMoTaW will have nearly unchanged yield strength and ductility at 1600 °C relative to untreated NbMoTaW.
Hf-modified NbMoTaW will retain the irradiation resistance predicted for untreated NbMoTaW.
Hf contents above approximately 0.5 at% may promote secondary-phase formation or alter BCC lattice parameters.
Secondary-phase formation or altered lattice parameters could compromise high-temperature strength or irradiation performance.
The proposed Peierls-barrier mechanism is plausible based on analogous Hf-containing alloy systems.

contradictions.description: The baseline calls irradiation resistance a known property, whereas the initial state and predicted outcome describe it as only predicted, and the uncertainty field states that its retention after Hf addition remains experimentally uncertain.
